newsitem.title: ALGERIA: FEATURE - After years of violence, signs of change in Algeria.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - After years of violence, signs of change in Algeria.

text.p: Rachid Touil, a former left-wing student leader, wandered through the streets of Algiers -- a nostalgic personal trip but also a symbol of hope and change for a new Algeria.

One of thousands of secularists who were lucky enough to find a provisional exile abroad, he was both testing Algerian leaders' claims to have turned the tide against Moslem guerrillas and assessing business opportunities.

Touil's return coincided with the election of Algeria's first pluralist National Assembly (lower house), with President Liamine Zeroual's supporters boasting that the relatively violence-free June poll was a new step towards ending nearly six years of strife and social upheaval.

Rachid, now a 40-year-old businessman living in Canada with his Algerian wife and two children, said he was back home to help his North African homeland switch from its 30-year-old centrally commanded economy.
"I'm here to boost Algeria's exports -- some of its manufactured products -- not to sell imported goods," he said after introducing his four foreign partners.
Touil and his partners were among a score of potential foreign investors staying at a main Algiers hotel to tap what diplomats see as Algeria's huge business possibilities.
"What happened this month is very encouraging for businessmen who are hoping to see this political momentum followed by a reduction of the violence," said a senior Western diplomat.
He said Algeria's leaders had achieved considerable progress in the past three years, capped by the early June multi-party general election.

"When foreign businessmen, who've been used to hearing that a civil war was ripping through Algeria, see that not one of about 8,000 candidates was killed during three weeks of poll campaigning and nearly threequarters of voters cast their ballots, this augurs well," he said.
But his five, heavily armed Western bodyguards standing by his bomb proof car suggest Algeria still has some way to go to tame violence.
OTHER SIGNS OF CHANGE
Still, there are other signs of change that have come in the shadow of the six years of violence in which about 60,000 people have been killed.
Paralleling that violence have been moves to a market society from three decades of centralised control.
Ahmed, a 45-year-old father of three children, walked into a middle-class restaurant in central Algiers on Thursday night, offering roses and yellow flowers for sale.

Such a job would have been seen as an affront to dignity by most Algerians until the early 1990s when despite -- or perhaps because of -- huge foreign debts the state made it easy to get a relatively well paid job.
"I'm an office clerk in the day beside selling flowers at night. Money became hard to get and it's not easy to make ends meet," he said.
At the far end of the small street where the restaurant is located, two young men watched passers-by.
"No, we're not plainclothes police. We are here to get some money by watching out for anyone suspicious round here and alerting the restaurant owner," said one. "But it is quiet now."
In another sign of the times, young men and women are filling newspapers with marriage advertisements -- insisting that the would-be partner has a stable job and comes from a good family.

Whatever the changes, a slogan sprayed on a wall above a group of young men playing dice and exchanging jokes on a street corner in Scalla district, on the heights of the Algerian capital, summed up the prevailing sentiment for many of the young:
"A visa! Let me go".
